section_summary: This concluding section finishes Mauricio Hochschild’s survey of South American mineral production and exports to Japan, then turns chiefly to American petroleum exports and the developing export-control regime in mid-1941. State Department memoranda, congressional and public correspondence, and industry reports debate whether oil shipments sustained Japan’s war effort, while documenting licensing delays, tanker capacity, and California export volumes. The section also covers potash exports, British handling of Japanese ships seeking fuel at Callao, and arrangements for a mining-company representative to meet Department officials.

subfiles.title: Continuation of Mauricio Hochschild’s report on South American mineral production and shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Hochschild explains why Bolivian, Peruvian, Argentine, Brazilian, and Chilean minerals continued to be sold to Japan and proposes that the United States purchase and store strategic ores itself.
subfiles.summary: The continuation reviews antimony, tin, tungsten, lead, zinc, copper, molybdenum, and beryllium production and trade in Bolivia, Peru, Argentina, and Brazil. Hochschild says Japanese buyers offered better prices, accepted impure ores, and possessed cheaper and more available shipping than American purchasers. He describes efforts to redirect tungsten and beryllium toward the United States and argues that cutting off Japanese purchases without replacement markets would close mines and cause political disruption. He recommends United States government purchasing, shipping, and storage programs and offers his firm’s cooperation.

subfiles.title: Shipments of Bolivian ores and concentrates to Japan, January 1940–April 1941
subfiles.about: A table records Bolivian mineral shipments to Japan by the Banco Minero de Bolivia and other suppliers.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure tabulates shipments of antimony, wolfram, lead-silver, copper, and asbestos from January 1940 through April 1941. It distinguishes Banco Minero de Bolivia shipments from those of other exporters and notes that the bank’s totals include ore supplied by M. Hochschild S.A.M.I.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Watson, Geach and Company’s supplementary mineral-shipment data
subfiles.about: Finletter acknowledges supplementary statistics on Peruvian and Chilean ore shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter confirms receipt of Mr. Geach’s June 17 communication supplementing Mauricio Hochschild’s June 5 report. The Department expresses appreciation for information covering Peruvian and Chilean shipments from January 1940 through April 1941.

subfiles.title: Forwarding supplementary mineral-shipment material to William L. Clayton
subfiles.about: Finletter forwards a Watson, Geach and Company letter and statistical data supplementing Hochschild’s mineral report.
subfiles.summary: Finletter encloses for Clayton’s information a copy of a Watson, Geach and Company communication together with its statistics. He identifies the material as supplementary to Mauricio Hochschild’s letter of June 5.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Gulf Oil Corporation concerning lubricating-oil exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Gulf Oil executives ask whether the Department objects to a cash sale of low-grade lubricating oil to Mitsubishi for shipment in Japanese tankers.
subfiles.summary: B. P. Newton and David Proctor state that Gulf Oil wishes to cooperate with the government and seek guidance about a proposed lubricating-oil sale to Mitsubishi. They explain that payment would precede loading, Japanese tankers would carry the oil, and no metal containers were involved. Mr. Adams cites American support for China but says the Department did not seek to induce a private moral embargo on unlicensed petroleum products. Gulf Oil was therefore told to exercise its own discretion under the existing regulations.

subfiles.title: Senator James M. Mead to Secretary Harold L. Ickes on oil exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Mead urges Ickes to oppose petroleum exports that he believes strengthen Japan and divert supplies from American and Allied defense.
subfiles.summary: Mead cites a Joseph Driscoll newspaper article and growing public concern over shipments of American oil to Japan. He argues that petroleum should be reserved for domestic defense and friendly nations rather than an Axis associate using it for war. Rejecting the contention that an embargo would drive Japan into the Dutch East Indies, he calls for an end to what he characterizes as appeasement and asks Ickes for his position.

subfiles.title: Acting Secretary Sumner Welles to Senator Mead on petroleum export controls
subfiles.about: Welles informs Mead that all petroleum-product exports have required licenses since June 20 and are reviewed for national-defense and foreign-relations effects.
subfiles.summary: Welles answers Mead’s June 19 letter after its referral by the Secretary of the Interior. He states that exports of all petroleum products have been prohibited unless licensed since June 20, 1941. Licensing decisions consider domestic supply, national defense, and relations with other powers, and he assures Mead that the issues raised are receiving careful attention.

subfiles.title: Harold R. Holmes to Joseph C. Green questioning continued oil shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Holmes asks an old acquaintance to explain why oil shipments to Japan continue despite the likelihood of their use against China or the United States.
subfiles.summary: Writing on Committee to Defend America by Aiding the Allies letterhead, Holmes sharply criticizes continued oil shipments to Japan and calls the policy appeasement. He contends that the oil may be used against China or the United States. The remainder of the letter exchanges personal news about their Princeton class, Bill Braddock, and Holmes’s work in Milwaukee.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green to Harold R. Holmes explaining petroleum-export policy
subfiles.about: Green denies that petroleum policy constitutes appeasement and explains the three categories of controlled and uncontrolled petroleum exports.
subfiles.summary: Green first exchanges news about Princeton classmates. He then explains that aviation gasoline and aviation lubricants had not been licensed for Japan, that lower grades had previously been licensed but not recently, and that the lowest grades remained outside export control. He emphasizes that the policy was repeatedly reviewed as circumstances changed and that press accounts had often been misleading.

subfiles.title: H. E. Steel protest against State Department shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: A Los Angeles correspondent denounces continued shipments of oil and war supplies through Japan as a betrayal of China, Britain, and American democracy.
subfiles.summary: Steel accuses the State Department of helping the Axis through continued shipments of oil and other war supplies to Japan. The writer contrasts official sympathy for China with policies allegedly harmful to China and Britain. The letter warns that broken promises could leave the United States fighting alone and that the public is awakening to the policy.

subfiles.title: G. S. Walden to Stanley K. Hornbeck on May petroleum shipments from California to Japan
subfiles.about: Walden reports preliminary May 1941 shipment volumes and current Japanese demand for California petroleum products.
subfiles.summary: Walden reports roughly two million barrels shipped from California to Japan in May, the highest monthly figure since July 1940, but attributes the increase to sailing schedules and three available whaling tankers. He says gasoline licenses had apparently not been granted for several months, while crude-oil licenses still moved with delay. Japanese purchases were limited chiefly by tanker capacity, with continuing demand for lubricating-oil distillate and selected crude but little interest in diesel or fuel oil.

subfiles.title: Stanley K. Hornbeck acknowledgment to G. S. Walden
subfiles.about: Hornbeck thanks Walden for information about May petroleum shipments from California to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck acknowledges Walden’s June 23 letter reporting on California petroleum exports to Japan. He states that the information is useful and expresses the Department’s appreciation.

subfiles.title: Potash Export Association notice of potash manure-salt shipment to Japan
subfiles.from: W. V. Gay, Potash Export Association, Inc.
subfiles.about: The association reports a recent shipment of run-of-mine potash manure salts to Japan and promises prompt reports of future exports.
subfiles.summary: The association advises that 2,041.96 short tons of potash manure salts averaging 24.94 units of potassium oxide per ton were shipped to Japan. It calculates the shipment as equivalent to 758.77 short tons of potassium oxide. The association promises to continue promptly notifying the Department of shipments to all destinations.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Potash Export Association shipment report
subfiles.about: Feis acknowledges the association’s report of potash manure-salt shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department thanks the association for its June 26 report of recent potash shipments to Japan. Feis notes the association’s intention to provide prompt notice of future shipments to all destinations.

subfiles.title: Dryden Linsley Phelps to the Secretary of State protesting American oil sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Phelps argues from China that rising American gasoline and oil sales to Japan undermine relief work and make the United States complicit in Japan’s destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: Phelps says reports of expanding American gasoline and oil sales to Japan have shocked Chinese readers and undermined confidence created by China Relief activities. He cites purported sales figures and argues that embargo and licensing announcements have misled American opinion about the trade’s continuation. Appealing to the Secretary’s reputation in China, he urges the United States to end its contribution to Japan’s war against the Chinese nation and its civilization.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the American Ambassador at Chungking concerning a reply to Dryden Linsley Phelps
subfiles.about: The Department sends Phelps’s letter to Chungking and supplies suggested language explaining American export-control law and petroleum restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The Ambassador is asked to acknowledge Phelps’s June 27 letter unless he sees an objection. Suggested text explains the Export Control Act of July 2, 1940, the process for designating strategic materials, and the licensing restrictions imposed on aviation fuel, aviation lubricant, and later petroleum products. It also stresses that China and Japan policy is determined by the entire United States government and must balance many legal, political, and national-interest considerations.

subfiles.title: Conversation with British Embassy officer concerning fuel for Japanese ships at Callao
subfiles.about: British and American officials discuss whether British oil companies should delay fueling five Japanese steamers at Callao, Peru.
subfiles.summary: W. G. Hayter reports that five Japanese steamers had made an unusual request for fuel at Callao and that the British Admiralty favored delay rather than outright refusal. The British Foreign Office also reported an apparent American Embassy request not to fuel the Norway Maru. After consulting Captain Schuirmann, Adams learned that the American naval attaché had merely offered to delay the ship and had been told that the Navy Department saw no advantage in doing so.

subfiles.title: Internal memorandum on gasoline export licenses for Japan
subfiles.about: An internal memorandum considers the political implications of either continuing to withhold or resuming licenses for higher-octane gasoline exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The writer infers from Walden’s attached letter that applications covering higher-octane gasoline were still being held up. Because the issue had become important, freely renewing licenses below 87 octane might appear to be a political concession to Japan. The memorandum concludes that a prompt decision was needed on whether withholding should continue.

subfiles.title: G. S. Walden to Stanley K. Hornbeck on Japanese gasoline purchases and California petroleum exports
subfiles.about: Walden describes Japanese demand for sub-87-octane gasoline, stalled license applications, company workarounds, and detailed May shipment figures.
subfiles.summary: Walden reports that Japan strongly wanted gasoline capable of reaching about 86–86.5 octane with added lead, but four months of inaction on licenses had nearly exhausted Pacific Coast suppliers’ authorizations. He describes Cities Service’s use of older Gulf licenses through purchases from Richfield and Standard Oil of California and reports total May shipments of 2,119,412 barrels, broken down by supplier and product. He attributes the high May total to sailing schedules and whaling tankers, estimates Japanese carrying capacity at about 50,000 barrels per day, and notes persistent demand and increasing scarcity for California lubricants. He also discusses possible diversion of Japan-bound cargoes to Dairen and the difficulty of filling lubricants into wooden barrels after restrictions on steel drums.

subfiles.title: Alger Hiss acknowledgment of Walden’s petroleum report
subfiles.about: Hiss acknowledges Walden’s July 10 report on Japanese petroleum purchases and May shipments from California.
subfiles.summary: Writing for Stanley Hornbeck, Hiss confirms receipt of Walden’s detailed July 10 letter. He expresses appreciation for the information concerning Japanese petroleum purchases and California’s May oil shipments.

subfiles.title: B. Elkan to the Secretary of State arranging a Washington meeting
subfiles.from: B. Elkan, International Minerals and Metals Corporation
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Thomas K. Finletter
subfiles.about: Elkan proposes a July 16 meeting with Finletter regarding the Compagnie Minière du M’Zaita at Chagres, Chile.
subfiles.summary: Replying to a Department letter of July 9, Elkan says he expects to be in Washington on July 16 and proposes a ten o’clock meeting. He asks to be advised in advance of any special information required and provides his Shoreham Hotel room as a contact if the time must be changed.
